## Overview

In this post, I explore the relationship between penguin body mass and flipper length across three penguin species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. I use Python to calculate summary statistics, visualize the relationship between measurements, and compare average body mass across species.

The data come from the [Palmer Penguins dataset](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/), collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The dataset is available through the `palmerpenguins` Python package.

## 1. Load and explore the data

First, I import the necessary Python libraries and load the dataset. I inspect the first few observations to understand its structure.

```{python}
#| warning: false

from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

penguins = load_penguins()

print("Dataset dimensions:", penguins.shape)

penguins.head()
```

The dataset contains measurements of penguins, including their species, body mass, flipper length, and bill dimensions.

## 2. Compare penguin size by species

Next, I calculate the average body mass and flipper length for each species. Missing measurements are excluded from the calculations.

```{python}
species_summary = (
    penguins
    .groupby("species")[["body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm"]]
    .mean()
    .round(2)
)

species_summary
```

These summary statistics allow us to compare the typical body mass and flipper length of the three species.

## 3. Visualize body mass and flipper length

I use a scatter plot to investigate the relationship between flipper length and body mass. Each species is represented separately to make comparisons easier.

```{python}
#| label: fig-penguin-size
#| fig-cap: "Relationship between flipper length and body mass across three penguin species."
#| warning: false

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))

for species in penguins["species"].dropna().unique():
    subset = penguins[
        penguins["species"] == species
    ]

    ax.scatter(
        subset["flipper_length_mm"],
        subset["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.7
    )

ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.set_title("Penguin Body Mass vs Flipper Length")
ax.legend(title="Species")
ax.grid(alpha=0.2)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The scatter plot illustrates a positive association between flipper length and body mass. Penguins with longer flippers generally have greater body mass, although the measurements vary within each species.

## 4. Identify the species with the largest average body mass

Finally, I use the summary statistics to identify which species has the largest average body mass.

```{python}
largest_species = species_summary["body_mass_g"].idxmax()

largest_mass = species_summary["body_mass_g"].max()

print(
    f"{largest_species} has the largest average "
    f"body mass: {largest_mass:.2f} g."
)
```

This calculation provides a direct comparison of average body mass across the three species.

## Conclusion

The analysis demonstrates how Python can be used to explore and summarize biological measurements. The species-level statistics show differences in average body mass and flipper length, while the scatter plot reveals a positive relationship between these measurements.

Gentoo penguins have the largest average body mass among the three species in this dataset. The analysis also demonstrates how grouping, aggregation, and visualization can help identify patterns in real-world data.
